hmmt-feb-2003-alg-01.title: Complete the square
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-01.body:
The condition is $x\ge 14\sqrt a-a$ for every $a\ge0$, so $x$ must be at least the maximum of $14\sqrt a-a$. Write $14\sqrt a-a=49-(\sqrt a-7)^2\le 49$, with equality at $a=49$. So the smallest valid $x$ is $49$.

**Answer: 49**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-02.title: Multiply by $\cos^2 20^\circ$
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-02.body:
Multiply numerator and denominator by $\cos^2(20^\circ)$. The numerator becomes $\sin^2 20^\circ-\sin^2 20^\circ\cos^2 20^\circ=\sin^2 20^\circ(1-\cos^2 20^\circ)=\sin^4 20^\circ$. The denominator becomes $\sin^2 20^\circ\cdot\sin^2 20^\circ=\sin^4 20^\circ$. The ratio is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-03.title: Count factors of 5
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-03.body:
Trailing zeroes of $n!$ equal the exponent of $5$ in $n!$ (there are always more factors of $2$), which is $\lfloor n/5\rfloor+\lfloor n/25\rfloor+\lfloor n/125\rfloor+\lfloor n/625\rfloor+\cdots$. Without the floors this is about $n/4$, so try $n\approx1160$: $232+46+9+1=288$. Moving to $n=1170$ gives $234+46+9+1=290$, while $n=1165$ gives $233+46+9+1=289$. The count first reaches $290$ at $n=1170$ (the count only jumps at multiples of $5$).

**Answer: 1170**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-04.title: Denest the root
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-04.body:
$2\sqrt{1.5+\sqrt2}=\sqrt{6+4\sqrt2}=\sqrt{6+2\sqrt8}$. Since $(\sqrt2+\sqrt4)^2=2+4+2\sqrt8=6+2\sqrt8$, this equals $\sqrt2+2$. Subtract $1.5+\sqrt2$: the result is $2-1.5=\tfrac12$.

**Answer: $\tfrac12$**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-05.title: Sum minus count
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-05.body:
The given sum equals $(n_1+2n_2+\cdots+2003n_{2003})-(n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_{2003})=(\text{sum of the numbers})-(\text{number of numbers})=2003-(\text{number of numbers})$. To maximise it, minimise the count of numbers. The words \"several\" and \"their\" mean there are at least two numbers, so the minimum count is $2$ (for example $1$ and $2002$), giving $2003-2=2001$. (If a single number $2003$ were allowed the value would be $2002$; this was the answer in the original key before a successful protest during the contest.)

**Answer: 2001**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-06.title: Induction on odd $n$
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-06.body:
Compute $a_1=1$, $a_2=\lfloor 8/1\rfloor=8$, $a_3=\lfloor27/8\rfloor=3$. Claim: $a_n=n$ for every odd $n$. Suppose $a_n=n$ for some odd $n\ge3$. Then $a_{n+1}=\lfloor (n+1)^3/n\rfloor=\lfloor n^2+3n+3+1/n\rfloor=n^2+3n+3$, and $$a_{n+2}=\left\lfloor\frac{(n+2)^3}{n^2+3n+3}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor n+2+\frac{n^2+3n+2}{n^2+3n+3}\right\rfloor=n+2,$$ because $(n+2)^3=(n+2)(n^2+3n+3)+(n^2+3n+2)$ and the remainder $n^2+3n+2$ is less than the divisor $n^2+3n+3$. Hence the claim holds by induction and $a_{999}=999$.

**Answer: 999**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-07.title: Use the equation itself
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-07.body:
Each root satisfies $x^3=-x^2+333x+1001$. Summing over the three roots: $a^3+b^3+c^3=-(a^2+b^2+c^2)+333(a+b+c)+3003$. Here $a^2+b^2+c^2=(a+b+c)^2-2(ab+bc+ca)=1+666=667$, so the sum is $-667-333+3003=2003$.

**Answer: 2003**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-08.title: Telescoping
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-08.body:
The $n$th term (starting at $n=3$) is $\dfrac1{n^2+(n-2)}=\dfrac1{(n+2)(n-1)}=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac1{n-1}-\dfrac1{n+2}\right)$. Summing from $n=3$, the terms $\frac1{n-1}$ run over $\frac12,\frac13,\frac14,\frac15,\ldots$ and cancel against $\frac1{n+2}$ over $\frac15,\frac16,\ldots$, leaving $\dfrac13\left(\dfrac12+\dfrac13+\dfrac14\right)=\dfrac13\cdot\dfrac{13}{12}=\dfrac{13}{36}$.

**Answer: $\tfrac{13}{36}$**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-09.title: Exponent of 2 in the central binomial coefficient
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-09.body:
Let $f(N)$ be the exponent of $2$ in $N$. By Legendre, $f\left(\binom{2n}{n}\right)=\sum_{k\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{2n}{2^k}\right\rfloor-2\sum_{k\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{2^k}\right\rfloor$. Since $\lfloor 2n/2^k\rfloor=\lfloor n/2^{k-1}\rfloor$, this equals $n-\sum_{k\ge1}\lfloor n/2^k\rfloor$. If $2^m\le n<2^{m+1}$ the sum has terms only for $k\le m$ and $\sum_{k=1}^m\lfloor n/2^k\rfloor\le n(1-2^{-m})$, so $f\ge n/2^m\ge1$ with equality exactly when $n=2^m$ (otherwise $f\ge2$). Therefore $\frac12\binom{2n}n$ is odd exactly when $n$ is a power of $2$ and even otherwise. There are $10$ powers of $2$ in $[1,1000]$ ($1,2,\dots,512$), so the answer is $1000-10=990$.

**Answer: 990**

hmmt-feb-2003-alg-10.title: Factor out roots
hmmt-feb-2003-alg-10.body:
Cross-multiplying: $(x+7)P(2x)=8xP(x+1)$. Comparing leading terms of a degree-$n$ polynomial with leading coefficient $c$ gives $2^nc=8c$, so $n=3$. Setting $x=0$ shows $P(0)=0$, so $P(x)=xQ(x)$ and $(x+7)Q(2x)=4(x+1)Q(x+1)$. Setting $x=-1$ gives $Q(-2)=0$, so $Q(x)=(x+2)R(x)$ and $(x+7)R(2x)=2(x+3)R(x+1)$. Setting $x=-3$ gives $R(-6)=0$, so $R(x)=(x+6)S(x)$. Degree $3$ forces $S$ constant: $P(x)=cx(x+2)(x+6)$. From $P(1)=1$: $21c=1$. Then $P(-1)=\frac1{21}(-1)(1)(5)=-\frac5{21}$.

**Answer: $-\tfrac5{21}$**
